title: The Eyes of Max Carrados
author: Based on Ernest Bramah
introText:
London, 1914. You are Max Carrados, the blind detective whose other senses have grown extraordinarily acute through forty years of use.

A telegram has arrived. A railway signalman named Hutchins is accused of causing a fatal accident at Knight's Cross Station. He swears the signal showed clear — but twenty-seven people are dead and the inquiry convenes tomorrow.

Something is wrong with this case. The sighted investigators have missed what only you can find.

Your friend Louis Carlyle sits opposite, the case papers rustling in his hands. The familiar smell of old books and beeswax fills the room.

locations.name: Title Screen
locations.description:
The Eyes of Max Carrados
     Based on Ernest Bramah
     London, 1914

     A DAAD Adventure

locations.name: Carrados's Study
locations.description: The leather of your armchair is warm beneath your hands — shaped precisely to you after forty years of use. The room comes to you through its signature: old books, beeswax polish, the cooling residue of last night's fire. The electric lamps are running at full power; you feel their warmth on your face as always. Carlyle's breathing tells you he is agitated. He has been turning the same page for ten minutes.

locations.name: Richmond Terrace
locations.description: The winter air cuts sharply after the warmth of the study. Your feet find the familiar texture of the front steps — three down, then the gravel path, then the pavement. The city announces itself: horses, wheels on cobbles, a steam whistle somewhere to the south. Parkinson is already at the motor car; you can hear the soft creak of leather as he straightens to attention.

locations.name: Motor Car (Richmond)
locations.description: The Dorvelle closes around you like a familiar glove. The leather seat, the smell of polished wood and motor oil, the particular sound the door makes when Carlyle pulls it shut behind him. Through the partition, Parkinson shifts in the driver's seat, awaiting your instructions. The city noise muffles to a distant hum.

locations.name: Klondyke Street, Holloway
locations.description: Coal smoke is the first thing — thick and domestic, the smell of a street where every chimney works hard against the cold. The pavement beneath your feet is uneven, worn down by decades of heavy boots. Children's voices carry from a yard nearby. Someone is frying onions. Number 107 is before you — you can hear movement inside the house.

locations.name: Motor Car (Holloway)
locations.description: The motor car sits at the kerb. The neighbourhood comes to you through its sounds: a woman calling from somewhere above, the slow clop of a milk horse passing, children's voices circling the car with curiosity. Parkinson says nothing to them. He never does.

locations.name: Hutchins Kitchen
locations.description: A kitchen scrubbed within an inch of its life — the smell of carbolic soap and coal smoke and something baking. The table is old but the surface is clean and smooth beneath your hands. A kettle mutters on the range. Someone has put out the good cups. Hutchins is standing — you can tell by the elevation of his voice, the way his weight shifts constantly from foot to foot. A man who cannot bring himself to sit in his own home.

locations.name: Hampton Court Street
locations.description: After the city and the industrial flatness of Woundy, the air here is almost startling — green and damp and alive. Birdsong. Real birdsong, not the urban sparrow variety but something more unhurried. The pavement gives way to packed earth under your feet. The neighbourhood carries wood smoke and wet leaves. Mead's cottage is here. You stand on the path for a moment, listening. The cottage is very quiet.

locations.name: Motor Car (Hampton)
locations.description: Parkinson has parked beneath what must be a large tree — you can hear the branches moving overhead and feel the occasional drop of moisture on the roof. The contrast with the city is complete. Carlyle is quiet beside you, which means he is thinking. You are thinking too.

locations.name: Mead's Cottage
locations.description: The cottage carries the particular smell of anxious tidiness — fresh soap overlaying everything, applied this morning more thoroughly than habit requires. A clock ticks on the mantel with mechanical precision. Mead is to your right — you can tell by the direction of his breathing, shallow and controlled, and by the slight displacement of air when he shifts his weight. A man who has rehearsed this conversation many times.

locations.name: Mead's Workshop
locations.description: Without Carlyle, the room takes on a different quality. The working silence of a space that is usually occupied. The air carries machine oil and metal dust and something sharper beneath them — precise and chemical. Tools clink softly on a rack to your right, still settling after the disturbance of the door. The floor changes texture under your feet: stone flags first, then the gritty resistance of metal filings, then fine wood shavings near the bench ahead.

locations.name: Woundy Station Platform
locations.description: The cold hits you as you step onto the platform — a different kind of cold than the city, rawer and damp. The rails hum faintly with the vibration of a distant train running somewhere on the network. Creosote and engine smoke have soaked into the very wood beneath your feet. The signal box is east of here. You have been in a hundred signal boxes. You know exactly what to search for in this one.

locations.name: Motor Car (Woundy)
locations.description: Your motor car in the station yard at Woundy. The smell of railway — coal smoke, hot metal, creosote — is thick in the air. Somewhere beyond the yard, a goods train moves slowly, its rhythm felt as much as heard through the ground. Parkinson keeps the engine idling against the cold.

locations.name: Knight's Cross Signal Box
locations.description: The box is empty — the inquiry has suspended normal operations here. The equipment fills the small room with its own music: the tick and click of the block instruments, the occasional mechanical sigh of the lever frame. The levers themselves are cold iron under your hands, smooth with years of handling. The smell of oil and metal is thick. And something else — a faint trace of something chemical, not quite right, beneath the familiar smell of the place.

locations.name: City Street
locations.description: The City comes at you from every direction — rapid footsteps on stone, the rustle of newspapers, fragments of urgent conversation about yields and margins. The smell of cigar smoke and printer's ink and horses and ambition. Pendleton's office is in the building before you — you can feel the edge of the stone steps with your stick.

locations.name: Motor Car (City)
locations.description: The City traffic surrounds you — the particular mix of iron wheels on cobbles and rubber tyres and hooves that tells you this is the financial district. A newsboy's voice cuts through, announcing something about railway stocks and recovery. In your pocket: a letter, three receipts, a diagram.

locations.name: Pendleton's Office
locations.description: The office announces itself before Pendleton speaks. The smell of burned paper beneath the cigar smoke — he has been destroying documents. A cold draught enters from somewhere to your right, a window left open despite the weather to clear the smell of burning. His chair scrapes quickly when he hears you announced — the movement of a startled man. His voice, when it comes, is too large for the room. You find a chair without being shown to one and sit down. You hear Pendleton register this and decide not to comment. Good. He is already making mistakes.

locations.name: Signal Row
locations.description: A dull thoroughfare of substantial elderly houses running parallel with the railway line. The cutting is deep here -- you can feel the vibration of passing trains through your feet. The houses have the particular smell of places that let rooms: carbolic, boiled cabbage, and respectability. One has a board with raised letters: ROOMS TO LET.

locations.name: Miss Chubb's Room
locations.description: A fair-sized room on the first floor. The window faces north -- you can feel the draught and hear the railway cutting below. The room has been cleaned but carries traces of its last occupant. The window frame has small screw-holes where something was recently mounted.

locations.name: Motor Car (Signal Row)
locations.description: Parkinson waits in the car on Signal Row. The sound of trains in the cutting is loud here.

locations.name: Long Acre Lamp Shop
locations.description: A small specialist shop smelling of brass polish and lamp oil. Glass discs of various sizes hang on a rack, chiming softly when you pass. The shopman watches you with the patient attention of someone who remembers unusual orders.

locations.name: Motor Car (Long Acre)
locations.description: The motor car on Long Acre, surrounded by the sounds of coach-builders and lamp-makers.

locations.name: Pendleton's Flat
locations.description: A well-appointed set of rooms in Mayfair. The carpet is thick beneath your feet, the furniture heavy and expensive. The air is saturated with cologne. A desk stands by the window. A wardrobe against the far wall. The fireplace has been used recently — you can smell ash. Parkinson waits on the landing outside.

locations.name: Motor Car (Mayfair)
locations.description: Parkinson pulls up on Curzon Street. Number 23 is ahead — a respectable building with a black door. Parkinson checks his watch and takes his position at the entrance. The street is quiet.

locations.name: The Hearing Room
locations.description: A formal chamber smelling of old wood and authority. The Board of Trade inquiry has reconvened. You can hear the rustle of papers, the creak of chairs, the particular quality of a room full of people trying to be quiet. Hutchins is here -- you recognise his breathing, steady now. Carlyle sits beside you.

objects.description: A common white-wood ruler. Your fingertips find a mark at four and seven-eighths inches, pressed deeper than the rest. Someone measured this distance many times. The same measurement as the signal glass.
A piece of lamp glass with edges too clean for an accident. Measured, scored, cut deliberately.
Stock certificates on heavy parchment. Purchase dates: three days before the crash. Sale dates: one week after. A fortune made from twenty-seven deaths.
A telegram on rough postal paper: MR CARRADOS STOP DESPERATELY NEED HELP STOP HUTCHINS
The Morning Herald, with articles about Knight's Cross and railway stocks.
Louis Carlyle, your trusted friend and most reliable interpreter of the visible world.
Parkinson, your loyal driver. Steady breathing, efficient movements.
Hutchins, the accused signalman. His breathing is grief and fear, not guilt.
Iver Mead, railway guard. His calm is deliberate, practised. He is hiding something.
Harold Pendleton, stockbroker. Expensive cologne over fear-sweat.
A heavy workbench, immovable. The wood surface records years of deliberate work.
A rack of tools: six chisels, two hammers, four files. Hung in deliberate order.
A heavy leather apron stiff with dried compounds. Machine oil and something sharper beneath.
A section of the bench front concealing a hidden drawer.

A letter on heavy City stationery. The handwriting is bold and threatening: 'If you value your family, you will say nothing of what you saw. This is not a request.' The paper carries cigar smoke and expensive cologne — the same cologne you have followed across London.
Three bank receipts bearing the seal of the Bank of England.
Rolled card with embossed engineering lines. A measurement in the corner: four and seven-eighths inches.
Margaret Hutchins, the driver's daughter. Young, composed, wearing a plain gold brooch and a gun-metal watch. She has decided not to break down in front of strangers.
A small wooden catch hidden under the bench lip, painted over but detectable by touch.
The Evening Herald. The financial pages tell a different story from this morning.

A visiting card on heavy stock. The name has been torn away — deliberately, you think, the edge is too clean for carelessness. But the address is printed: 14 Threadneedle Street. And the cologne. Expensive, sharp, utterly distinctive. You will know this scent again.
Miss Chubb, the landlady. A bustling woman who finds the world slightly unsatisfactory but is determined to manage it.
A carbon copy. Green glass disc, four and seven-eighths inches diameter. Paid cash. The paper carries that same cologne.
The lamp-maker. Careful hands, a good memory for unusual orders.
Mr Greatorex, Carrados's secretary. A precise, efficient man who reads the morning papers and manages correspondence. He places no interpretation on what he observes — only reports.

A collection of Greek and Roman bronzes, arranged on a side table. Each piece is known to your fingers — the weight, the patina, the particular warmth of genuine antiquity versus the cold precision of forgery. You are one of the foremost authorities on numismatic forgeries in England.

A cedar box of cigars — the most desirable and unobtainable variety, procured through connections that Carlyle has never quite understood. The smoke is rich, complex, and entirely unlike the crude cologne that has occupied your attention these past days.

rules.name: Carlyle follows - Knight's Cross Signal Box
Carlyle follows - Long Acre Lamp Shop

actions.text: A new morning. The case papers are spread across your desk.

Parkinson appears. 'I observed Curzon Street yesterday evening, sir. The daily woman departs at noon. The gentleman returns at approximately six-thirty. The flat is unoccupied between noon and half past six.'
The third morning. Carlyle has already left to meet Pendleton for luncheon. Parkinson waits with the car.
Carlyle introduces himself. 'Routine questions for the inquiry, Mr Pendleton.' Pendleton's voice is too large for the room -- confidence worn like armour.
You stand on the first-floor landing. The door to the flat is locked. Parkinson waits beside you, his hands steady.

The inquiry is brief. You present the evidence. The glass proves tampering. The ruler and order slip prove premeditation. The stock certificates prove motive. The letter proves conspiracy. And the cologne -- traced across London -- proves one man was at every scene.
Mead testifies, his voice unsteady. Pendleton threatened his family. The chairman nods slowly. 'The evidence is overwhelming.'
Hutchins is cleared. His record restored. As you leave, his hand grips yours -- rough, callused, trembling. He says nothing. He does not need to.

In the motor car, Carlyle is quiet. Then: 'How did you know, Max?' You smile. 'I listened, Louis. The signal was clear. Someone simply made certain that clear looked like danger.' Carlyle: 'The blind detective sees what sighted men miss.'

*** THE END ***

Ending A: Full Justice
Pendleton convicted. Hutchins restored. Mead protected.
You present what you have. The glass proves tampering. But there are gaps. Pendleton's solicitor argues circumstance. The chairman frowns.

'Hutchins is cleared. Regarding Pendleton, the evidence is suggestive but this board recommends further police investigation.' Pendleton adjusts his cufflinks. He knows. You know. But knowing is not proving.

*** THE END ***

Ending B: Partial Justice
Hutchins cleared. Pendleton referred but not convicted.
You needed more evidence.
The glass proves tampering. Hutchins is cleared. But the chairman looks at you. 'And the saboteur, Mr Carrados?' You have no answer that would stand in court.
Somewhere in the City, Pendleton orders another cigar. He knows. You know. But knowing is not proving.

*** THE END ***

Ending C: Hollow Victory
Hutchins cleared. The saboteur walks free.
Two sharp knocks on the door. Parkinson's voice, low: 'I would suggest we do not linger, sir.'
Three rapid knocks. 'Sir! Someone on the stairs. We must go now.' You gather what you have and move quickly to the door. Parkinson is already leading you down the back staircase.
You address Carlyle.
You address Hutchins.
You address Margaret.
You address Mead.
You address Pendleton.
You address Miss Chubb.
You address the shopman.
You address Greatorex.
You step back from the conversation.
Carlyle reads the financial pages. Railway Deferred fell nine points. Someone bought before and sold at the peak. 'Harold Pendleton,' Carlyle says. 'A stockbroker. I heard his name at my club.'

Carlyle describes the scene. 'A high blank wall on one side. On the other -- houses. The signal would be visible from upper floors.' He pauses. 'If someone wanted to study this signal, they would need a room with a view of it.'
Without Carlyle you rely entirely on your hands and nose. The room speaks through texture and scent. Your fingers read surfaces like a language only you can speak.
'Carlyle,' you say, 'describe what you can.'
You stand still and let the room speak. Your hands, your ears, your nose -- forty years have made them more reliable than any pair of eyes.
A carbon copy. Green glass disc, four and seven-eighths inches. Paid cash. The paper carries that cologne.
A visiting card on heavy stock. The name has been torn away. But the address is printed: 14 Threadneedle Street. And the cologne -- expensive, sharp, memorable.
Beneath the carbolic and coal smoke, something else. Faint but unmistakeable -- an expensive cologne. Not Hutchins's. Someone else has been here recently.
Oil, metal, creosote -- honest smells. But beneath them: that cologne again. The same one. Whoever visited Hutchins was also in this signal box.
The cologne is stronger here than anywhere. This was where its owner spent hours. The same scent -- at the kitchen, at the signal box, and now here.
Machine oil and metal dust. And there -- the cologne. It clings to the leather apron. Whoever wore this was at every scene.
The cologne hits you the moment you enter. Not a trace -- a cloud. The same scent you have followed across London. The man who planned twenty-seven deaths is sitting three feet from you.
The cologne is everywhere. This is where he lives, where he planned twenty-seven deaths.
You breathe in carefully. Nothing unusual draws your attention.
A solid door. Good wood, brass fittings. But the lock is simple — the kind of lever lock that a man with the right skills could manage in moments. Parkinson has such skills.

Parkinson produces a slim leather case from his inside pocket. He works the lock with a practised hand — no fumbling, no hesitation. The bolt turns. He pushes the door open. 'I shall wait here on the landing, sir. If anyone comes up the stairs, I will knock twice.' You step inside. The cologne is immediate and overwhelming.
The door is locked. You need to get inside first.
Even through the closed door, you can smell cologne. Expensive. Distinctive. The same scent you have followed across London.
You are on the landing. A locked door. Parkinson beside you. The cologne seeping through the gap beneath the door.
Solid wood. Brass fittings. A simple lever lock. Parkinson could open this.
Your hands move across the desk. In the top drawer: stock certificates. Purchase dates three days before the crash. Sale dates one week after.
Expensive clothes. A City overcoat with machine oil and metal dust on the cuffs. He wore this to the signal box.
Ash from burned papers. But fire is not thorough -- a fragment survives. A receipt from a lamp-maker. Long Acre.
You have no reason to visit Holloway yet.
You don't know enough about the signal yet.
You need to examine the signal box evidence first.
You have no business in the City yet.
You have no reason to visit the houses near the signal. Not yet.
You have no reason to visit lamp makers. Not yet.
You cannot go to Pendleton's flat without ensuring he is elsewhere.
You need to address someone first. TALK followed by their name.
They don't seem to have anything to say about that.
Carlyle pauses. 'Not sure what you're driving at, Max.'
'Not sure what you're driving at, Max.'
'Not sure what you're driving at, Max.'
'No name -- torn off. But the address is printed: 14 Threadneedle Street.' 'What's there?' 'Stockbrokers. Several firms share the building.'
'This is precision work, Carlyle. A lamp-maker.' 'Long Acre. If someone ordered custom glass, that's where they'd go.'
'I made enquiries. Pendleton keeps rooms at 23 Curzon Street, Mayfair. Lives alone. Daily woman leaves at noon.'
'I'll have Parkinson observe the building this evening.' Parkinson inclines his head. 'Very good, sir.'
'Invite Pendleton to luncheon. Keep him occupied.' Carlyle understands. 'I'll use the inquiry as pretext. He can't refuse.' 'Parkinson and I will be at Curzon Street.'
'Not sure what you're driving at, Max.'
Hutchins shifts his weight. 'I don't know about that, sir.'

Margaret speaks quietly. 'There was a man who came. Three weeks ago. Father was not home. He dropped this.' She presses a card into your hand. The name is torn away. But the cologne is sharp and distinctive.
Margaret shakes her head quietly. 'I'm sorry, I don't know about that.'
Mead's calm is deliberate. 'I have nothing to add to what I told the inquiry.'
Pendleton waves a hand dismissively. 'I really can't help you with that.'
Miss Chubb brightens. 'The gentleman! Very particular about a north-facing room. Expensive cologne. Left rather suddenly after the railway accident. Left a ruler in the drawer upstairs.'
'His cologne! I could smell him from two floors away. It's still in the room. I've aired it three times.'
'First floor, north-facing. Go through there.' She gestures east.
Miss Chubb shakes her head. 'I'm sure I wouldn't know about that.'
The shopman remembers. 'Green glass disc, four and seven-eighths inches. Said it was for a signal lamp. Paid cash. Gentleman in expensive cologne.' He produces a carbon copy.
'Very distinctive. I'd know it anywhere. Not our usual customers.'
'I'm afraid I can't help with that, sir.'
Carlyle grips your arm. 'Max. We have nothing. Not even proof the signal was tampered with.'

'We have him, Max.' You lay it out: the glass, the ruler, the order slip, the certificates, the letter, and the cologne at every scene. Pendleton collapses. 'I want my solicitor.' Carlyle: 'The police are already on their way.'
'It may be enough,' Carlyle says quietly. 'It may not. We have gaps.' You make your decision.
Carlyle: 'We can prove tampering but we can't prove he did it. We need more.'

Parkinson pulls into the traffic. 'Tell me about Hutchins,' you say. Carlyle opens the file. 'Forty-three years old. Fifteen years on the Knight's Cross route without incident. His supervisor calls him meticulous.' 'And yet,' you say. 'And yet,' Carlyle agrees.
Parkinson navigates the familiar route to Holloway. The streets narrow, the air thickens with coal smoke.

Parkinson drives to Woundy Station. The smell of railway — coal smoke, hot metal, creosote.

Parkinson drives to Hampton. The air is greener here, away from the city.

A soft tap on the door. 'Still clear, sir. But I would suggest efficiency.'

You step into the cottage. Mead is standing — you hear his weight shift as he sees what you carry. Then his voice breaks. 'He said he would hurt my family. I saw him at the signal box that night. I was afraid.' His breathing is ragged. 'I should have spoken. I know that now.' Carlyle is already reaching for his notebook.
Your armchair. Forty years of use have shaped it to you. You have solved eleven cases in this chair.
A large desk, partners style. Everything has a specific location known by distance and angle from the near left corner.
Scrubbed pine, the grain raised by years of washing. A peaceful house — or it was, until three nights ago.
The kettle mutters on the range. Someone put it on when they heard you at the door — the reflex of a household that receives guests properly even in catastrophe.
Cold iron, each lever in its correct position, paint worn by generations of signalmen. Someone subverted this mechanism.

A heavy desk by the window. The surface is cluttered — you can feel papers, a pen tray, a blotter. The top right drawer yields to your touch.

The study is warm after the December cold. Parkinson has laid dinner. The electric lamps blaze at full power — your characteristic touch of irony, visitors are told. You settle into your armchair and reach for the bronzes on the side table. Your fingers find the small Donatello — the one that isn't a Donatello, though it took you three years to prove it.

'Greatorex,' you say. Your secretary appears at the door. 'The Evening Herald, sir. I have marked the financial pages.' 'Read me the railway stocks.' Greatorex reads. The Central and Suburban Deferred fell nine points. 'Now read me the three days before the crash.' A steady rise. Someone was buying.

Carlyle sets down his glass. 'The cologne, Max. You mentioned a cologne.' 'The same cologne. At Hutchins's kitchen, where a visitor came three weeks ago. At the signal box, where someone tampered with the lamp. I will find it again before this is finished.' You light a cigar. The smoke rises, clean and honest — nothing like the scent you are hunting.

Dinner is quiet. Parkinson serves and withdraws. Carlyle eats without tasting. The letter from Mead's workshop lies between you on the table — Pendleton's handwriting, Pendleton's threats, Pendleton's cologne.

'The man was terrified, Max,' Carlyle says at last. 'Mead. When he saw what you were carrying out of that workshop, his face...' He stops. 'I have seen guilty men. Mead is not guilty. He is a man who was given an impossible choice and chose silence.' 'And twenty-seven people died for that silence,' you say. 'Not for his silence. For Pendleton's greed.'

You reach for the Donatello again. The bronze is cool and familiar. 'Tomorrow I need Pendleton out of his flat. Invite him to luncheon at your club.' 'And while I keep him at table?' 'Parkinson and I will visit Curzon Street.' Carlyle is quiet for a moment. 'Max. If you are caught in a man's private rooms—' 'Then you will defend me admirably in court, Louis.' You smile. Carlyle does not.

You smoke the last of your cigar and listen to the fire settle. Tomorrow will be decisive. You turn the bronze in your hands — the false Donatello, the forgery that took three years to expose. Some deceptions require patience.

Your fingers move across the collection. Greek, Roman, Renaissance. Each piece has a story your hands can read — weight, patina, the temperature of the metal. The small Donatello is your favourite. It isn't a Donatello, of course. It took you three years to prove it. You are one of the foremost authorities on numismatic forgeries in England.

The most desirable and unobtainable cigars in London, procured through connections that Carlyle has never quite understood and Parkinson has never questioned. The cedar box is warm to the touch. The smell is rich and complex — nothing at all like the cologne you are hunting.

You select a cigar by touch, cut it precisely, and light it. The smoke rises. For a moment the world narrows to this — the warmth of the armchair, the crackle of the fire, the particular quality of tobacco that costs more than most men earn in a week. You think better when you smoke.

Mr Greatorex, your secretary. A precise and efficient man who arrives at ten each morning and reads you the papers. He marks what you want to hear and you clear off the morning news in no time. He reports what he observes without placing his own interpretation on it — a quality you value above all others in a secretary.

The fire has burned low. Greatorex has gone home. Parkinson moves quietly in the house, performing the small rituals of closing up. You sit in your armchair with the Donatello in one hand and a cigar in the other.

The evidence is spread across your desk. You have touched each piece a dozen times today: the glass, cut to four and seven-eighths inches. The ruler with its worn mark. The order slip from Long Acre. The stock certificates. The letter threatening Mead. And threading through all of it, like a signature in perfume — the cologne.

Carlyle appears in the doorway. 'The hearing reconvenes at ten tomorrow, Max. Will you be ready?' 'I have been ready since I smelled that cologne in Hutchins's kitchen,' you say. 'Everything since then has been confirmation.' Carlyle pours two brandies. 'To justice,' he says. 'To evidence,' you reply.

messages: The paper is cheap government stock, rough against your fingertips. The typewriter keys struck hard and fast — a man in a hurry, or a man afraid. You set the telegram down carefully. 'Someone wanted this crash, Carlyle. A disaster like this does not happen by chance — it happens by design. And design requires motive. What does this morning's Herald say about Knight's Cross?'

Carlyle reads aloud. The accident coverage is substantial -- twenty-seven dead, the inquiry, Hutchins's name prominent. Then the financial pages. Railway stocks fell sharply on the day of the crash and recovered within a week. Someone bought before the fall and sold at the peak. 'Someone who knew this crash was coming,' you say. Carlyle pauses. 'Harold Pendleton. A stockbroker in the City. I heard his name at my club -- he purchased heavily three days before the crash.' You stand. 'Then we begin with Hutchins. I want to hear the man's story. Holloway, Carlyle.'

'Harold Pendleton,' Carlyle says. 'A stockbroker in the City. I heard his name mentioned at my club last week in connection with a remarkably well-timed railway investment. I thought nothing of it at the time. He purchased heavily three days before the crash.' You stand. 'Then we begin with Hutchins. I want to hear the man's story in his own words before I form any further conclusions. Holloway, Carlyle.'

Your fingertips move slowly along the wood. The grooves are regular except at one point — at what your trained touch tells you is four and seven-eighths inches, the wood is worn fractionally deeper. This measurement was checked many times. 'Carlyle — the glass fragment. Measure it against this.' He takes both. A pause. 'Four and seven-eighths inches, Max.' 'Of course it is.' You are very still. 'Someone stood at this window and verified that measurement until they were certain. This was planned over days. Possibly weeks.'

You turn the fragment carefully in your hands. The edges are wrong — too clean, too regular for a break. Your fingertip follows the scored line, feeling the deliberateness of it. Cut with a tool. Measured. Intentional. 'It is an inside man, Carlyle. Someone with access to this box, knowledge of this lamp, and a very steady hand. The guard on duty that night was Mead.' You pocket the fragment. 'We go to Hampton.'

'Green, Mr Carrados.' His voice is quiet but absolutely certain. 'I have driven that route for fifteen years. I know that signal the way I know my own heartbeat. It was green. Clear. I brought her through at full speed because that is what a clear signal means. They do not believe me. Nobody believes me. But it was green.'

A long silence. The kettle mutters. Somewhere above, a child moves across the floor. 'Twenty-seven,' he says at last. The word has weight. 'I keep trying to learn their names from the papers. It seems wrong not to know them.' His voice does not break exactly, but it bends. 'I did not do it, Mr Carrados. I know that is what they all say. But I did not do it.'

'There was something...' He hesitates — the hesitation of a man who has been disbelieved once and fears it again. 'The lamp looked different that night. The green was brighter than usual. Too bright, almost. Cleaner. I mentioned it at the inquiry.' His voice hardens slightly. 'They wrote it down and moved on.' You are already very still. 'Brighter than usual. Not dimmer. Brighter.' 'Yes sir.' You stand. 'Carlyle — the signal box. Now.'

'Iver Mead? Good man. Solid. Known him eight years.' A hesitation. 'He was quiet before that shift. More quiet than usual. I asked if he was all right and he said he was. But he was not.' A pause. 'I should have pressed him. I know that now.'

'Pendleton?' He tries the name carefully. 'No sir. I do not know that name.' His voice is steady and untroubled. He is telling the truth. But his breathing carries something else — a residual tension that is not quite this question. There is more here. You will need to find the right way in.

She speaks before her husband can stop her. 'He is a good man, Mr Carrados. Whatever they say about him.' Then, quieter: 'There was a man who came to the house. Three weeks ago, perhaps four. George was not home. He said he had business with my husband. He waited. He smelled of money — expensive, very sure of himself. He left no name. George never mentioned anyone calling. I never told him. The man frightened me, though I could not have said why at the time.'
'I wasn't there,' she says. Her voice is steady but the steadiness costs her something. 'He came home at two in the morning. I heard the door. I did not go down.' A pause. 'I wish I had gone down.'

He is very quiet. 'A man came to see me,' he says at last. 'At work, not here. About three weeks before the accident. He had a proposal. He said that if I were to allow a certain signal to show incorrectly on a certain night, I would be well compensated. He said no one would be hurt.' His breathing changes. 'I told him what he could do with his proposal. He left. I burned his card. I told no one — I had no proof and thought no one would believe a railway man over a City gentleman. I should have told someone. I know that now.'

'Everything was normal.' The words arrive smooth and rehearsed — too smooth. 'I carried out my duties as per regulations. The signals were operated correctly. I have nothing to add to what I told the inquiry. I am sorry about Hutchins. He is a good man. But I cannot help him.'

A change moves through the room — small but legible. Mead's breathing shifts: a microsecond of held breath, then released too carefully. 'I did not touch the lamp,' he says. 'That is not part of a guard's duties.' His voice is steady. His heartbeat is not. 'He is lying,' you say quietly to Carlyle, in French. 'About the lamp specifically. He knows exactly what happened to that lamp.'

'Pendleton?' The name lands in the room differently from the others. Mead's voice is controlled: 'I do not know that name.' But for one unguarded fraction of a second his breath stopped entirely. 'He knows that name,' you say to Carlyle, still in French, just below hearing. 'His body told me.' Carlyle asks again in English. Mead repeats his denial, steadier this time. But the damage is done.

'The workshop is private.' His voice carries something harder now. He moves — and by the displacement of air you know he has placed himself between you and the eastern door. 'There is nothing in there relevant to the inquiry. Nothing relevant to anything. I would like you to leave now, if you do not mind.'

Carlyle says pleasantly: 'Mr Mead, I should have mentioned at the outset — I am here in a semi-official capacity, retained by the inquiry board to collect supplementary statements from all personnel on duty that night. It is purely procedural, but it must be done properly, at a table, and it will take some time. Shall we sit?' You hear Mead's calculation — the pause of a man who cannot refuse a formal statement without appearing guilty. 'Yes,' he says finally. 'I suppose.' The sound of chairs. Mead moving away from the workshop door. You are already moving east.

Your hands move slowly across the bench surface — reading the scarred wood, the stains, the small geography of a working life. Then, at the front edge near the left corner, your fingers find something. A slight unevenness in the wood. Not a natural flaw — too deliberate for that. You press, and feel movement. A catch. Hidden under the lip of the bench, painted over but not quite flush. 'Found you,' you say quietly.

The catch gives under your thumb with a small, precise click. A drawer slides out from beneath the bench — not large, perhaps twelve inches by four, running on well-oiled runners. Someone has used this drawer regularly and recently. Inside: paper. Your fingers find a letter on heavy stock. Folded papers — several. And something rolled in stiff card. You take your time.
The drawer is already open. The papers are where you left them.

You hear them before you reach the door — Carlyle's measured voice putting a careful question about procedures, Mead's answers careful in a different way. You open the door and step into the cottage. Carlyle continues without pause — a professional reflex. But Mead stops speaking entirely. You cross the room with the documents secure in your inside pocket, and you can hear Mead's breathing change — short and rapid, the breathing of a man watching something inevitable arrive. 'Thank you for your time, Mr Mead,' you say pleasantly. He says nothing. His silence says everything.

Carlyle closes his notebook with a decisive snap. 'I think that covers everything we need for now, Mr Mead. The inquiry board will be in touch.' He rises smoothly. As he passes you he murmurs, almost inaudibly: 'His face, Max.' You are already at the door.

'Mr Carrados. And Mr Carlyle, is it?' His voice is too large for the room — the voice of a man who has decided that confidence is his last defensible position. 'I was not aware we had an appointment.' 'We had not made one,' you say pleasantly. 'We find appointments give people time to prepare. We prefer conversations to performances.' A fractional pause. Then Pendleton laughs — too loud, too long. 'Very good. Well. What can I do for you gentlemen?'

'A sound investment, nothing more. I study the markets carefully — that is my profession. I identified a structural weakness in the railway sector and acted accordingly.' His voice is loud, fluent, well-practised. 'Many investors made similar purchases at that time.' 'Did they,' you say. It is not a question.

'I do not know anyone by that name.' The denial came before you had quite finished saying the name. You file that away precisely. 'Iver Mead,' you say. 'Railway guard. Knight's Cross section. Ten years service.' 'I have told you. I do not know him.' The cologne is very strong. Beneath it, the first faint trace of fear-sweat — there since before you arrived, but stronger now.

The silence that follows has shape and weight — the silence of a man who has just seen something he feared was coming. When Pendleton speaks his social fluency has gone. 'I do not know what you mean.' 'I think you do,' you say. 'The lamp at Knight's Cross signal box. The glass removed and replaced with a piece cut to four and seven-eighths inches. The piece that made a red signal read as clear at distance. Measured with a wooden ruler that is now in my pocket.' Another silence. Then Carlyle steps forward. 'Mr Pendleton, I must insist you account for the timing of your stock purchases in full. I have the inquiry board's authority and I intend to use it.' Pendleton turns toward Carlyle. His attention locks.

Carlyle steps forward with the particular energy he reserves for moments requiring controlled aggression. 'Mr Pendleton, I must insist you provide a complete accounting of your railway stock transactions for the period in question. I have the inquiry board's formal authority to demand this, and I intend to use it.' Pendleton turns toward the voice. You are already moving.

You move quietly around the room while Carlyle's argument fills the space between them. A man with a stick, apparently finding somewhere comfortable to stand. Pendleton does not attend to you. Your fingers find the desk. You begin at the top left corner and work methodically. Correspondence, nothing relevant. A pen tray. A blotter. Then, top right, a leather folder. Inside: official paper, an embossed seal of the stock exchange, and here — typewritten dates you can trace without difficulty. Three days before the accident. You close the folder quietly and slip the document into your inside pocket. 'Mr Pendleton,' you say, interrupting Carlyle. 'I owe you an apology. I told my colleague I expected to find the certificates in the top right of your desk. I was wrong — they were in a folder. I am usually more precise.'

Pendleton stares. 'You searched—' 'Your desk,' you confirm. 'While you were attending to Carlyle. A man with a stick, moving around a room, does not draw the same attention as a man with two working eyes. It is one of the condition's few advantages.' You place the certificate on the desk between you. 'The date of purchase. Three days before the accident you arranged. The letter detailing your instructions to Mead and your threats against his family. The receipts documenting your payments to him. The diagram showing the exact measurement you calculated for the glass. The ruler from the signal box confirming that calculation was executed precisely. And the glass itself.' You stop. 'Twenty-seven people, Mr Pendleton. Shall I go on?' The silence that follows is the longest you have heard in a long career.

CONGRATULATIONS. You have solved the Knight's Cross Signal Problem. Harold Pendleton will face justice for his crimes, Mead for his reluctant complicity. And Hutchins — innocent Hutchins — will keep his job and his freedom. Pendleton does not confess. Men like Pendleton rarely do, not immediately. But he does not deny either. He sits down heavily and says nothing at all, and in that silence his guilt is as plain as anything you have ever read with your hands. The blind detective sees what sighted men missed.

You need more before you can make this accusation formally. The ruler and glass establish the method. The certificate establishes the motive. You need the evidence from the workshop connecting Pendleton to Mead directly — the letter, the receipts, the diagram. Without those, Pendleton walks free. 'I will return, Mr Pendleton,' you say pleasantly. 'Please do not go anywhere.'
'Not yet, Carlyle. I need to understand what we are walking into before we walk into it. There is more to learn here first.'
'The signal box can wait. I want to hear Hutchins tell his story in his own words first. A man's voice tells you things a report cannot. I am not ready for the signal box yet.'
'I am not ready to face Mead yet. I need to understand the method before I confront the man who used it. The signal box first.'
'I have suspicion, Carlyle, and suspicion is worthless in a court of law. I need what is in that workshop before I face Pendleton. We are not finished at Hampton.'

Mead has positioned himself between you and the workshop door. The displacement of air is unmistakeable. He will not allow you through without a reason to look elsewhere. You need Carlyle to give him one.
Pendleton is watching the desk too carefully. You need Carlyle to occupy his attention before you can search it.

Parkinson pulls into the traffic and you settle back, the city moving around you in sound and smell. 'Tell me about Hutchins,' you say. Carlyle opens the file. 'Forty-three years old. Started on the railway at sixteen. Fifteen years on the Knight's Cross route without incident. His supervisor describes him as meticulous.' 'And yet,' you say. 'And yet,' Carlyle agrees.

'Brighter than usual,' Carlyle repeats, as Parkinson navigates south. 'What does that mean precisely, Max?' 'It means someone replaced the red glass in that signal lamp with a piece calculated to allow enough light through to read as clear at distance. Red light through clear glass at the right width produces exactly that effect — brighter, cleaner, wrong. That requires knowledge of the mechanism. And access to the box.' 'An inside man,' you confirm. 'Let us go and see what he left behind.'

The motor car moves through quieter streets. 'Mead had access,' Carlyle says, 'and Mead was frightened before his shift, and Mead's pulse changed when I mentioned a certain name this morning.' 'You suspected before we left the study,' Carlyle says. 'I suspected. Suspicion is not evidence. Evidence is what we are going to find.'

You sit in the motor car with the documents in your inside pocket. 'Read me the letter,' you say. Carlyle reads. Pendleton's words, Pendleton's threats. 'He was certain he would never be caught,' you say. 'He did not plan for a blind detective.' 'No,' Carlyle says quietly. 'They rarely do.' 'The City, Parkinson.'

The motor car turns back through familiar streets toward Kensington. The city changes around you as you move — the sound of it softens, the smell shifts from commerce to coal smoke and cooking. But the case is not finished.

'The bare facts, Max. A collision at Knight's Cross three nights ago. Twenty-seven dead, nineteen injured. Engine-driver Hutchins claims the signal showed clear. The inquiry convenes tomorrow morning. If Hutchins cannot produce an explanation he will be held responsible — his licence revoked, possible criminal proceedings. He has no explanation. Only his word.'

'Fifteen years on that route without incident. Exemplary record. Known to be careful, methodical, not a drinking man. His colleagues speak well of him.' Carlyle's voice carries a note of frustration. 'By every measure he is exactly the kind of man who does not make this kind of mistake. And yet twenty-seven people are dead.'

'The 11:42 from Paddington. Hutchins brought it through Knight's Cross at full speed — the signal showed clear, he says. But the signal was red. The train struck a goods wagon on the main line.' Carlyle stops. 'It was very bad, Max.'

'Harold Pendleton. Stockbroker, City of London. Moderately successful until recently — there were rumours of difficulties. Then three days before the Knight's Cross accident he purchased a significant quantity of railway stock at depressed prices. Sold it a week after the crash at considerable profit.' A pause. 'It may be coincidence.' His tone suggests he does not believe it.

'Iver Mead. Railway guard, ten years service. The guard on duty at Knight's Cross the night of the accident. He was responsible for the signals in that section. The inquiry has not focused on Mead. Hutchins is the easier target.'
'Carlyle,' you say, 'describe what you can.' He clears his throat and begins — the particular methodical description he uses when he knows you need information rather than impressions.

There is no one here to be your eyes. But you do not need eyes for this room. You have something better: forty years of learning to read the world through your hands and ears and nose. Stand still for a moment. Listen to what the room has to say.

Your armchair. Forty years of use have shaped it precisely to you — the leather worn smooth at the armrests, the cushion settled at the exact angle you prefer. You have solved eleven cases in this chair. You settle back and feel, as you always do, that thought comes more easily here than anywhere else.

Three walls, floor to ceiling — you know this from the particular acoustic quality of the room, the way sound behaves. Your fingers find the nearest shelf. Every spine carries a small adhesive marker in the corner, braille-coded in your own system. Yours is organised by usefulness.

Three electric lamps at full power — you feel their warmth on your face and hands, a gentle steady radiation. Your housekeeper once asked why a blind man needed so much light. You told her it was for visitors. This is not entirely true.
A large desk, partners style, inherited from your father. Everything has a specific location known by distance and angle from the near left corner. The telegram is at the front.

The cobblestones of Richmond Terrace are as familiar as furniture. You know the slightly raised stone three paces from the gate, the place where the kerb drops an inch lower than it should. You could manage it at speed in any weather.

You rest your hands on the table surface. Scrubbed pine, the grain raised fractionally by years of washing. The edges are worn round by elbows and forearms across two decades. This is a peaceful house. Or was, until three nights ago.

The kettle mutters on the range with the comfortable sound of something about to boil. Someone put the kettle on when they heard you at the door — the reflex of a household that receives guests properly even in the middle of a catastrophe. Nobody has yet moved to make the tea.
You lift one carefully. Bone china — you can tell by the weight and the faint resonance when you set it back down. The good cups. Brought out for company. This household has not given up.

You crouch and rest two fingers briefly on the nearest rail. Cold iron, and beneath the cold a faint vibration — a distant train running somewhere on the network. This particular line has carried a message that twenty-seven people read too late.

Old timber, deeply impregnated with creosote — you can smell it with every breath and feel the slight roughness through the soles of your shoes. The platform has its own acoustic quality: sound travels differently here, less enclosed than a building, more directed than open ground.

The lever frame runs the width of the box — you count them by touch, moving along the row. Cold iron, each lever in its correct position, the paint worn away by the grip of generations of signalmen. Someone in this box subverted that mechanism. The thought has a quality of cold that has nothing to do with the temperature.

The block instruments tick and click with bureaucratic precision — recording the movement of trains, the occupation of sections of track. They were doing this on the night of the accident. The instruments do not lie. Someone took care to ensure that what they recorded was itself a lie.

You move carefully along the floor near the lamp housing, your stick preceding you. Splinters of glass, small and sharp. And here: two parallel impressions in the accumulated dust where something rested on the floor. A case or bag, set down while someone worked. The marks are precise. This was not improvised.

A mantel clock — you can identify the maker by the particular cadence of the tick, a double beat with a slight emphasis on the second. An expensive movement for a railway guard's cottage. The sound of it fills the room with a regularity that is almost confrontational in these circumstances.

Your fingers find the antimacassar on the nearest chair back. Fresh laundering — the stiffness of something dried quickly, possibly this morning. Someone cleaned this house thoroughly and recently. People clean their houses when they are expecting something to happen.

Cold grate. In weather like this the fireplace should have been lit this morning. Your fingers find the ash — cold, undisturbed. Mead has been in a state of mind today where ordinary domestic warmth did not occur to him. He has been waiting.

A plain door, heavier than interior doors usually are. When you move toward it, Mead moves too — the displacement of air is unmistakeable. He has been tracking your position since you arrived and placing himself between you and this door throughout.

You move slowly across the floor, attending to what your feet tell you. Stone flags at the entrance. Then the surface changes: gritty underfoot, a faint metallic quality — metal filings embedded in the stone over years of work. Then near the bench, fine wood shavings. And here, near the left corner, a patch where the floor has been scrubbed recently and more thoroughly than the rest.

The apron hangs on a peg just inside the door. Heavy leather, stiff with dried compounds. Machine oil, predominant. Then something sharper — chemical, precise, in the family of things used in fine work. And beneath that, almost gone but not quite: the residue of an expensive cologne. You have encountered that cologne before.

You reach out to the wall. Papers, pinned there — you can feel the edges of several sheets. Engineering drawings, by the weight and stiffness of the card. You take one down. Embossed lines — a technical diagram. Precise angles. Dimensions you cannot read. But the nature of the drawing is clear to you, and it confirms what you already know about this room and this man.

'I can describe what I observe, Mr Carrados.' Carlyle pauses. 'A well-maintained building. Fresh paint on the window surrounds. The garden path is tidy. The curtain at the front window has just moved.' Another pause. 'Someone inside has noted our arrival and chosen not to come to the door. And the side of the building — a path around the left side leading to a separate structure at the rear. A workshop, by the look of it.' 'A workshop,' you say. 'Almost certainly.'

Well tended — your feet find no weeds on the path, the edges are defined. There is a particular smell to a cared-for garden in winter: cold earth, the ghost of last summer's plants. Today you notice only that the path to the workshop has been recently used. The earth is disturbed.

Recently used — the warmth is still faintly perceptible, and the smell of burned paper is strongest here. You crouch and feel the grate. Ash, still slightly warm. Pendleton has been burning documents this morning. He has not been busy enough.

Open, despite the cold. Someone wanted air circulation, or wanted the smell of burning to dissipate. It has not dissipated. 'He knew we were coming,' you say quietly to Carlyle. 'He has been expecting something ever since the accident.'

'Certificates,' Carlyle murmurs. 'Framed. Professional qualifications, memberships of various institutions. A photograph of Pendleton with someone official-looking.' He pauses. 'He needs people to know he is legitimate.' 'Men who are legitimate,' you say, 'rarely need to advertise it quite so thoroughly.'

The City comes at you from every direction — rapid footsteps on stone, the rustle of newspapers, fragments of urgent conversation about yields and margins. Twenty-seven people died in a railway accident three nights ago. Here it has already become a line in a financial report.
A boy's voice, close and sharp, announcing something about railway stocks and recovery. The word recovery. In your pocket: a letter, three receipts, a diagram. Someone else's idea of a recovery.
Carlyle has already read you the relevant sections. The railway stocks. The timing. The name.

A document on heavy parchment, stiff and formal under your fingers. The embossed seal of the stock exchange in the top corner. The typewritten dates leave impressions you can trace: three days before the accident; nine days after. A purchase and a sale, timed with knowledge that could only have come from certainty of what was going to happen.

Heavy paper, expensive — you can tell by its weight and the faint crackle when you flex it. An embossed address at the top: something in the City. The typewriter impressions are deep and forceful throughout. The paper carries the residue of cigar smoke and, very faintly, the same cologne you have now encountered twice.

Three folded papers, each identical in weight and texture. Each bears an embossed seal in the upper corner — the Bank of England, unmistakeable. Three payments. Three dates. The paper is of the quality associated with substantial transactions.

Rolled card, stiff. An engineering drawing — you unroll it and let your fingers read the embossed lines: parallel edges, precise angles, a cross-section of some housing. And in the corner, a single measurement your fingers trace with complete recognition. Four and seven-eighths inches.

Louis Carlyle — lawyer turned inquiry agent, your most reliable interpreter of the visible world. His breathing is slightly elevated, his weight forward in the chair. The case troubles him more than he is saying. It troubles you too.

A large man — his voice comes from above your own height and his footsteps on the kitchen floor are heavy and deliberate. His hands are calloused in the way of men who handle iron levers daily. His breathing is rapid but not evasive — the breathing of grief and fear, not guilt.

Iver Mead, railway guard. His breathing is shallow and controlled — the deliberate calm of a man who has been practising it. His weight is slightly forward on his feet. The smell of machine oil is present on his hands even through the soap.

Harold Pendleton, stockbroker. A large man — his movements displace the air in the room when he shifts his weight. His cologne is expensive and generously applied. Beneath it: fear-sweat, faint but unmistakeable, present since before you arrived.

A heavy bench, immovable. The wood surface is a record of years of work: burns, gouges, chemical stains, the smoothed channels where tools have been laid repeatedly in the same positions. Your hands move slowly across it, reading its history. There is something here.

You touch each tool in turn. Six chisels, graduated in size, edges recently sharpened. Two hammers, a heavy and a light. Four files, their surfaces rough and purposeful. Everything hung in a specific order. The arrangement of a man who knows where each thing is without needing to search for it.

Mrs Hutchins. A faint draught from the direction of the window tells you where she stands, and her breathing — quiet, controlled, effortful in its control — tells you who she is. She believes her husband. She has decided not to break down in front of strangers.
Carlyle gives you a blank look. 'What stocks, Max? We have not yet established a financial motive. Perhaps we should read the Herald first.'
You cannot find any way to open it. You need to examine it more carefully first.
You cannot locate a catch. Run your hands along the workbench first.
Air currents stir the hanging tools, making them chime. You count by sound alone: six chisels, two hammers, four files. 6-2-4. The numbers are deliberate.

The leather apron is stiff with dried compounds. Machine oil first, then something sharper — chemical, precise. And beneath that, almost gone but not quite: the residue of an expensive cologne. You have encountered that cologne before, on a man whose fear-sweat it failed to mask.
The air carries machine oil and metal dust and something sharper beneath them — precise and chemical. And there — faint, almost gone — the ghost of expensive cologne.
You have already retrieved the certificate from the desk. It is safe in your pocket.
Hutchins looks puzzled. Perhaps there is someone else here who knows something.

A section of the bench front that is not quite right — the wood slightly proud of the surface around it, the grain interrupted. A drawer, concealed rather than locked, built to be missed rather than found. It has no handle you can detect.
A small wooden catch beneath the lip of the bench, painted over but not flush with the surrounding wood. It moves under your thumb with a small, precise resistance — and then gives.
